# The Heat Is Uneven: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Summer heat has always been a fact of urban life, but climate change is transforming a seasonal nuisance into a public health emergency. Cities are inherently hotter than their surroundings—the urban heat island effect can raise urban temperatures by several degrees Fahrenheit compared to nearby rural areas, because asphalt, concrete, and dark rooftops absorb sunlight and re-radiate it long after sunset. The consequences are not evenly distributed. Heat deaths in the United States now exceed those from hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined, and they concentrate in specific neighborhoods: those with few trees, aging housing stock, and residents who cannot afford air conditioning. The question of how to make cities bearable in summer is therefore not merely a matter of comfort or engineering. It is a question of justice, urban design, and the tradeoffs that residents must weigh when heat solutions compete with other pressing needs.

## Trees: The Oldest and Best Technology

The single most effective intervention against urban heat is also the most ancient: shade.
